doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Roswell and Shreveport: Iceland refused, segregation
summary: He cannot be posted to Iceland because he is black, chooses Shreveport, and describes segregated towns near bases in Roswell, Montana and Louisiana.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years

blocks.x: I says, “yeah, sign me up.” I wanted to get out of Roswell, New Mexico. That’s where we were. We were in Roswell, New Mexico.
Man I’ll tell you, you’ve been to some of the hot spots.

Oh definitely. That’s where they have the UFO sightings or something. And by the way in Roswell I had some experiences too, like social things. Like they had a sign up on the wall that says, “we refuse the right to serve anyone.” I mean I was a GI, you know, off base there trying to have a little fun with my buddies and that was on the wall. And the same thing happened in Montana by the way. That’s almost, that’s not too far from the border you know. So in each place I had a little touch of that social problem.
Did that attitude also include your fellow military people?

If it did I didn’t notice it too much. I don’t know why I didn’t pay too much attention, it was just something I just didn’t notice. I guess I was lucky that way. Not unless I had a direct confrontation. If I had a direct confrontation then I would sort of listen to it and ignore it somehow. I don’t know why but it just went on. It came out in the music I guess. Because now that you ask that question I did have an experience with a guy that I went on leave with once. He was a bagpipe player up in Montana. And we were going along

and he was from Tennessee. And he said, “do you know what a nigger is?” That type of thing. And I just sort of dismissed it. Boom. Gone. That’s the only direct thing that I can recall during that time. But back to Roswell, they said, “well Iceland, we could ship you up there.” And then they found out that I was black and they says, “we don’t have any black GI’s up there.” So I couldn’t go to Iceland. So instead I chose Shreveport, Louisiana, which was just as bad. So I went to Shreveport and everybody was fine on base. The problem was off-base because the city ordinances, yeah. Whites and blacks couldn’t sit on the same row, in the front together or in the back together. One had to be in the back, if he was going to work you know what I mean. And I had another thing that happened there, while I was in this spirituality thing. I had a fellow that used to come up to the air base once a week, because I couldn’t go, and be with the group, because of the laws. And they are all white see? But anyway he would come out to the base, and he was a captain and I was a little, whatever it was, two or three stripes. And he’s walk in the barracks and everybody would snap to. And he’d say, “hey John, how are you?” Yeah. That type of thing. Because he was there to help me with my — we’d find some place, a corner or somewhere, and we’d talk, or a building. And we’d talk about spiritual things. And he did that for as long as I was there at the air base.
